images.title: Line up the matching primes
images.purpose: Show the HCF of 225 and 750 as the primes the two factorisations share, lined up column by column.
images.composition: Two rows of square prime tiles sit in the centre, aligned in six columns, with the matched columns framed and one result line below; wide white margins all round.
exact_structure: Six aligned columns of square tiles, in order from left to right: column 1 for 2, columns 2 and 3 for 3, columns 4, 5 and 6 for 5.
Top row, row label 225 on the left: tiles in columns 2, 3, 4 and 5 only, reading 3, 3, 5, 5; exactly 4 teal #0072B2 tiles; columns 1 and 6 are empty slots.
Bottom row, row label 750 on the left: tiles in columns 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 only, reading 2, 3, 5, 5, 5; exactly 5 amber #E69F00 tiles; column 3 is an empty slot.
Exactly 3 columns, column 2 (a 3 above a 3), column 4 (a 5 above a 5) and column 5 (a 5 above a 5), are each enclosed by one tall rounded reddish purple #CC79A7 frame around both tiles.
One result line centred below the rows: HCF = 3 × 5 × 5 = 75.
rejection: a tile count other than 4 tiles for 225 and 5 tiles for 750
a frame around any column that does not have a tile in both rows, or other than exactly 3 frames
images.takeaway: Only the primes that appear in both numbers, as many times as both have them, make the HCF.
images.description: Prime tiles for 225 and 750 lined up in columns; one 3 and two 5s are matched in both rows, giving HCF = 3 × 5 × 5 = 75.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on finding the HCF of 225 and 750 by minimum counts.
images.teaching_notes: Count the framed columns: each one is a prime both numbers have, so the 2 and the third 5 are left out.

image_decisions.why: Lining up the two factorisations shows exactly which primes are shared and how many times.
